facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The serial site, situated in the state of Rajastahan, includes six majestic forts in Chittorgarh; Kumbhalgarh; Sawai Madhopur; Jhalawar; Jaipur, and Jaisalmer.
facts.text: UNESCO inscribed Kumbhalgarh Fort as a World Heritage Site in 2013 under the serial nomination Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The second longest wall is a disputed statement as there has not been enough citation in this regard. Rajasthan Tourism is made it as its USP in one of the advertisement.
facts.text: Popular travel lore describes Kumbhalgarh as the second longest continuous wall in the world after the Great Wall of China, but military historians and archaeologists dispute this ranking by citing longer ancient fortifications such as Iran's 195-kilometre Great Wall of Gorgan and Pakistan's Ranikot Fort.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to the legend, all the efforts to build the wall of the fort failed, every time the wall was built, it would collapse as the construction proceeded.
facts.text: Local Mewar folklore recounts that during initial construction, the fort walls collapsed repeatedly each night until a spiritual priest declared that only a voluntary human sacrifice could remove the impediment.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: When no volunteers came forward Mer Baba offered his own head to the king.
facts.text: According to local legend, a wandering ascetic named Baba Bhairon offered himself to Rana Kumbha to be ritually beheaded so the fort's masonry could stand undisturbed.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: A small Hanuman mandir was built at the spot where the saint's severed head had fallen, to commemorate his great sacrifice. The gate made next to the mandir was named Hanuman Pol.
facts.text: Mewar lore states that the entrance gateway named Hanuman Pol was erected at the precise location where the severed head of the sacrificed ascetic landed.
